What to include:
- the presenting complaint and its history: onset, cause or mechanism, duration, site and side, character, what makes it better or worse, what has been tried
- relevant past history, medications, allergies, and social or risk factors
- pertinent negatives: things the patient denied, or the clinician noted as absent
- examination findings and test results
- the diagnosis or impression as stated, keeping any hedging ("probably", "rule out")
- every part of the plan: medications, referrals, tests, follow-up, and safety-netting advice

What to leave out: greetings, small talk, thanks, identity checks, scheduling or dictation housekeeping, and general explanations, unless they carry something clinically important for this patient.

How to write each point:
- One point per clinical item, written at the level a well-written note would state it. Keep together the details that belong to one item: a medication with its dose, frequency and duration is one point; an examination finding with its site and side is one point; how an injury happened is one point.
- Do not merge separate items: two different medications, two different findings, or a plan and its safety-net advice are separate points.
- Do not list the same item twice, for example once from the history and again from a later summary by the clinician.
- Make each point readable on its own, without the transcript, and keep it under 30 words.
- Keep negation, hedging and conditions exactly as said: "denies numbness", "call back if it does not improve".
- Give a short verbatim quote (at most 25 words) from the transcript as evidence, copied word for word. Use "..." only to join two parts of the same passage.

Grade the consequence of the omission for the patient and for the next clinician who reads the note. Grade the omission, not how dramatic the topic sounds. Grade each fact on its own, as if it were the only thing missing from an otherwise complete note.

## Grades

- the diagnosis or working impression, or a hedge on it (a "possible" diagnosis recorded as certain is just as serious)
- any drug, dose, frequency, duration, allergy or interaction
- a condition attached to the plan ("only if it gets worse")
- safety-netting advice: when to return, call, or seek urgent care

- a pertinent negative the management decision rests on (no fracture on X-ray, so no immobilisation beyond a splint)

- onset, timing, mechanism or character details that colour the picture without deciding the plan

- background history or social context with no immediate action attached

- small talk, rapport, thanks, administrative or dictation housekeeping ("order the medications we discussed")
- general education phrasing
